what_happened: The job was about speeding up Athena's test check. The reading was corrected by the operator (the "brain"). The correction gave measured timings: a cold compile takes 67 s and a warm-build run takes 673 s, so running the tests dominates, not compiling. It named the slowest test binaries. It said to prefer cargo-nextest, pinned by version and checksum in athena.toml [tools], with doctests run separately. It said to apply this to the test check, CI and the producer guidance. It said to record the measured numbers in the decision entry. It added a fallback of splitting the slowest binaries if nextest cannot be installed. The original reading did not match what the user meant, so the operator had to supply the diagnosis, the chosen tool and the constraints.
cause: Athena's reading of a speed-up request is built without a measured stage timeline. No step profiles where the time goes (compile versus run, per binary) before the reading fixes a method. Without that data the reading cannot pick the lever that matters (parallel test running rather than compile caching). It also cannot see that the tool must be pinned in [tools] like the others, or that doctests need a separate run. The operator measured by hand and wrote the method into the correction.
prevention: Add a measure-first step for any request to speed up a pipeline or check. Before the reading is accepted, Athena runs or reads a timing breakdown (compile versus run, per test binary or stage) and puts it in the reading. The reading must then name the dominant cost and justify the chosen lever against it. A reading that proposes a speed change with no recorded measurements is refused. The reading template for speed work should also list the standing constraints: tools pinned by version and checksum in [tools], every test still run (doctests), CI and producer guidance updated, and a stated fallback.
proposed_request:
Speed up Athena's test check, which is dominated by running the tests (about 673 s with a warm build) rather than compiling (about 67 s cold). Measured by the brain on this machine (4 cores, 2026-10-25): the slowest test binaries are athena-cli tests/lifecycle.rs 174 s, tests/job_plan.rs 83 s, tests/drain.rs 61 s, athena-core unit tests 61 s, tests/retry.rs 54 s, tests/steward.rs 48 s and tests/introspection.rs 36 s. Use cargo-nextest (buy-first) so individual tests run in parallel across binaries. Pin it by version and checksum in athena.toml [tools], like the other tools. Run doctests separately with cargo test --doc so every test still runs. Use this for Athena's test check, for CI and in the producer's guidance. Record the measured numbers in the decision entry, labelled as measured by the brain. If nextest cannot be installed in the sandbox, say so in the decision entry and fall back to splitting the slowest binaries' tests so they run in parallel. Acceptance:
- The test check, CI and the producer guidance all use nextest, and doctests run separately.
- The nextest pin is in athena.toml [tools] with version and checksum.
- The decision entry contains the measured numbers.
- The full test count is unchanged, with no test skipped.
- The new wall time of the test check is reported next to the 673 s baseline.
